title: Associations of food processing and dietary risk factors with colorectal cancer incidence in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study: A cohort study
one_line: A prospective cohort of 461,682 cancer-free US adults aged 50-71 at recruitment in 1995-96, followed a median 18.8 years to 10,075 colorectal adenocarcinomas, finding no association with total ultra-processed food intake and then decomposing UPF into its nutrient components.
key_claims: Total Nova group 4 intake showed no association with colorectal cancer: fifth versus first sex-specific quintile of energy-adjusted grams gave HR 0.97 (CI 0.91-1.03, p for trend 0.55), with proximal colon 1.02, distal colon 0.94 and rectum 0.91 all crossing one.
The null survived adjustment: adding Healthy Eating Index 2020 plus calcium and fibre, or BMI (kept in separate models as possible mediators), each gave 0.94, under a 10% change in estimate.

In this cohort UPF and guideline-recommended foods largely coincide: 82.8% of whole grain intake, 33.5% of fibre, 31.7% of calcium, 23.5% of dairy and 74.3% of processed meat came from UPF sources, with median UPF intake 293 g per 1,000 kcal per day, 43% of energy (IQR 36-50%).

Mutually adjusted continuous component analyses mirrored standard dietary guidance from both sources: calcium from UPF HR 0.77 per 300 mg/day (0.69-0.86) versus 0.90 (0.87-0.93) from non-UPF; dairy 0.75 versus 0.90 per serving; meat 1.08 versus 1.04 per serving.

Whole grain and fibre were the asymmetric case: from UPF sources HR 0.87 per serving of whole grain and 0.72 per 10 g of fibre, while their non-UPF counterparts in the same model were not significant.

Exploratory subgroups split as the decomposition predicts: bread 0.91, breakfast cereals 0.84 and frozen desserts/milk drinks 0.82 (all p for trend <0.001), against reconstituted meat and fish products 1.10 (1.04-1.18).

Substituting 10% of grams from ultra-processed to minimally processed food gave HR 0.98 (0.96-0.99) against 0.94 for the same substitution in EPIC — same direction, about a third the magnitude — which the authors attribute post hoc to composition (UPF meat 20.1 g/day here versus 36.2 in EPIC; breakfast cereal 15.2 versus 5.0; bread 57.3 versus 43.6).
limitations: The food frequency questionnaire (124 items, administered once) was built to estimate nutrients, not processing, so Nova assignment for ambiguous items such as yogurt comes from population-level consumption data applied identically to everyone, giving non-differential misclassification that pulls toward the null.

Validation against two 24-hour recalls gave a validity coefficient of 0.66 for energy-adjusted UPF grams in both sexes (and only 0.43 in men and 0.33 in women for unadjusted energy from UPF), so substantial attenuation remains even for the primary exposure.

No ingredient-level data, so emulsifiers, sweeteners and other additives were not estimated at all; the authors cite the emulsifier-and-gut-barrier literature and state plainly they could not test it.

A single 1995-96 baseline diet in a mostly white cohort aged 50-71; the authors write that their estimates likely underestimate current UPF intake and that limited variation across quintiles may itself contribute to the null.

The by-source analyses stack a second, less-validated classification layer on the first and are labelled exploratory, with the authors noting significant findings should be read cautiously given multiple testing.

The non-significant non-UPF whole grain and fibre estimates are most likely a precision problem — under 20% of whole grain intake was non-UPF — and the authors' narrower fibre argument (that the cohort's fibre signal has come from whole-grain fibre) is an interpretation, not a demonstration.
Proportional hazards were violated (score test p = 0.005), handled by estimating within five-year follow-up windows reported as generally similar.

High-UPF participants differed substantially (top versus bottom quintile: obesity 29.6% versus 15.2%, college 34.4% versus 41.8%, frequent exercise 40.6% versus 49.7%), which would bias away from the null, although the top quintile also had more nondrinkers (30.7% versus 21.5%); funding was the NCI Intramural Research Program with several authors employed by the funder, declared as having no role in design, analysis or publication.
open_questions: A cohort with repeated dietary assessment and ingredient-level additive estimates, showing whether any association survives adjustment for the nutrient components — the experiment that separates processing from content.
Repeat the whole-grain-by-source comparison in a population where non-UPF whole grain is commonly eaten, so that estimate has the precision to be compared.
Test the composition explanation for the EPIC discrepancy directly, since it is post hoc but testable.
Establish whether a null over a 36-50% energy-share contrast says anything about current intake levels.
